blocks.content: Not every LLD interview looks the same. Companies test design skills in four distinct formats and knowing which one you're facing before you walk in changes your entire preparation strategy.

blocks.content: 1. Type 1: Class design interview
Pure design no running code needed
Most common at product companies Flipkart, Swiggy, Uber, Google
You're given an open-ended system and asked to design its class structure. The interviewer wants to see how you think, not necessarily see code compile.
You sketch classes, define attributes and methods, establish relationships, and justify every decision.
The conversation is the product. Interviewers will push back, change requirements mid-session, and ask "what if we need to add X?" to see how your design handles change.
HOW THE ROUND FLOWS
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/9a1e430b-290e-4acd-ac51-cb839e1675ec.png

WHAT INTERVIEWERS LOOK FOR

Clear class responsibilities, correct relationships (composition vs aggregation), right design pattern applied, SOLID principles followed, and the ability to articulate every trade-off out loud.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 2. Type 2: Machine coding round
Write working code in 60–90 minutes
Most common at startups and mid-stage companies Razorpay, CRED, Zepto, Meesho

You receive a problem statement and must produce fully working, runnable code from scratch within the time limit. The code must compile, handle edge cases, and produce correct output when the interviewer runs it.
Design still matters a well-structured solution beats a working but messy one but correctness is the first bar you must clear.
WHAT HAPPENS INSIDE 90 MINUTES
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/5cf57a05-1f0b-407a-aff0-d3deb610f87b.png

THE HIDDEN BAR

Interviewers run your code after the round. A program that crashes on edge cases empty input, negative values, concurrent requests fails even if the class structure is beautiful.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 3. Type 3: Code walkthrough interview
Review, critique, and improve existing code
Common at senior engineer and tech lead levels Thoughtworks, Atlassian, Microsoft
The interviewer hands you a codebase usually a working but poorly designed system. Your job is to read it, identify what's wrong, explain why it's wrong, and suggest how you'd refactor it.

This format tests whether you can read code as fluently as you write it. You need to spot SOLID violations, unnecessary coupling, missing abstractions, and design pattern opportunities in someone else's code, under pressure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/a9568195-43b6-4d3e-9d96-0b0042f42dcd.png

WHAT TO LOOK FOR

God classes doing too many things, missing interfaces, hardcoded dependencies, no abstraction between layers, repeated logic that should be extracted.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 4. Type 4: Mixed format
Design first, then implement
Common at FAANG and larger product companies Amazon, PhonePe, Paytm

This is both Type 1 and Type 2 combined. You start by designing the class structure talking through entities, relationships, and patterns. Then, in the second half, you implement key parts of the design as working code.
It is the hardest format because it demands both breadth
(can you design a clean system?) and depth (can you actually build it?). Time management is critical spending too long on design leaves no time to implement.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/bebf5283-34b9-4217-8f5f-6d66d8900b6d.png

THE BIGGEST TRAP

Spending 50 of 80 minutes on design leaves you with no time to implement anything. Time box Phase 1 strictly even if the design isn't perfect, move to code. A working imperfect system beats a perfect unbuilt one.
blocks.title: Note

6. How to prepare for all four
blocks.text: 6. How to prepare for all four

blocks.content:
["Sketch Daily: Pick one real-world system every day and design its class diagram from scratch. Focus on identifying entities, relationships, responsibilities, and interactions clearly. Repeat this consistently until translating requirements into structured designs feels natural and automatic.
","Code Timed: Practice building complete working systems within a strict 75-minute time limit. Avoid extending the timer. This improves implementation speed, prioritization, and the ability to make solid engineering decisions under pressure. Always run and test your code before finishing.
","Read Code Critically: Explore open-source codebases with an analytical mindset. Intentionally look for SOLID principle violations, poor abstractions, tight coupling, and areas that could benefit from refactoring. Then think through how you would redesign those parts more effectively.
","Talk Out Loud: Explain your design decisions while you work, just as you would during a technical interview. Verbalize trade-offs, architecture choices, and reasoning behind your implementation. Recording yourself occasionally is surprisingly effective for improving clarity, communication, and confidence.
"]
items: Sketch Daily: Pick one real-world system every day and design its class diagram from scratch. Focus on identifying entities, relationships, responsibilities, and interactions clearly. Repeat this consistently until translating requirements into structured designs feels natural and automatic.

Code Timed: Practice building complete working systems within a strict 75-minute time limit. Avoid extending the timer. This improves implementation speed, prioritization, and the ability to make solid engineering decisions under pressure. Always run and test your code before finishing.

Read Code Critically: Explore open-source codebases with an analytical mindset. Intentionally look for SOLID principle violations, poor abstractions, tight coupling, and areas that could benefit from refactoring. Then think through how you would redesign those parts more effectively.

Talk Out Loud: Explain your design decisions while you work, just as you would during a technical interview. Verbalize trade-offs, architecture choices, and reasoning behind your implementation. Recording yourself occasionally is surprisingly effective for improving clarity, communication, and confidence.

blocks.content: BEFORE EVERY INTERVIEW
Ask your recruiter which format to expect. Most companies will tell you. Knowing in advance lets you walk in with the right mindset design thinking vs implementation speed vs code critique.
